claim: The simultaneous application of PET and MRI has revolutionized the ability to assess brain function across various physiological dimensions.
source: The simultaneous application of PET and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has revolutionized our ability to assess brain function across various physiological dimensions (Wehrl et al., 2013; Judenhofer et al., 2008).

claim: Combining PET with fMRI has opened many investigative avenues.
source: Combining PET with fMRI has opened many investigative avenues.
evidence: Based on established scientific understanding of multimodal imaging capabilities

claim: Resting-state functional connectivity (rs-FC) is a technique used in neuroscience.
source: Techniques such as resting-state functional connectivity (rs-FC) (Biswal et al., 1995) or pharmacological MRI (phMRI) (Jonckers et al., 2015) are now complemented by the ability of PET to quantify molecular changes, including alterations in receptor and transporter availability (Sander et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Biswal et al., 1995

claim: Pharmacological MRI (phMRI) is a technique used in neuroscience.
source: Techniques such as resting-state functional connectivity (rs-FC) (Biswal et al., 1995) or pharmacological MRI (phMRI) (Jonckers et al., 2015) are now complemented by the ability of PET to quantify molecular changes, including alterations in receptor and transporter availability (Sander et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jonckers et al., 2015

claim: PET can quantify molecular changes, including alterations in receptor and transporter availability.
source: Techniques such as resting-state functional connectivity (rs-FC) (Biswal et al., 1995) or pharmacological MRI (phMRI) (Jonckers et al., 2015) are now complemented by the ability of PET to quantify molecular changes, including alterations in receptor and transporter availability (Sander et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sander et al., 2013

claim: The BOLD signal in fMRI indirectly captures neuronal changes through neurovascular coupling.
source: The blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signal in fMRI indirectly captures neuronal changes through neurovascular coupling (Buxton, 2012), revealing only the hemodynamic consequences of molecular-level drug effects.
evidence: Supported by citation to Buxton, 2012

claim: The BOLD signal reveals only the hemodynamic consequences of molecular-level drug effects.
source: The blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signal in fMRI indirectly captures neuronal changes through neurovascular coupling (Buxton, 2012), revealing only the hemodynamic consequences of molecular-level drug effects.
evidence: Based on understanding of neurovascular coupling and the indirect nature of BOLD signal

claim: PET has been used mainly in pharmacological studies to illustrate quantitative shifts in neuroreceptor or transporter availability.
source: Typically, PET, used independently or simultaneously with fMRI, has been used mainly in pharmacological studies to illustrate quantitative shifts in neuroreceptor or transporter availability (Silberbauer et al., 2019).

claim: Several studies have explored the interregional coherence of PET tracer signals.

claim: Subject-level metabolic connectivity using [18F]FDG-PET has been established through the temporal correlation of regional PET signals.
source: While subject-level metabolic connectivity using [18F]FDG-PET has been established through the temporal correlation of regional PET signals (Wehrl et al., 2013; Amend et al., 2019), studies employing transporter or receptor tracers have focused predominantly on interregional binding coherence across subjects using static scans (Lanzenberger et al., 2012; Vanicek et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wehrl et al., 2013; Amend et al., 2019

claim: Studies employing transporter or receptor tracers have focused predominantly on interregional binding coherence across subjects using static scans.
source: While subject-level metabolic connectivity using [18F]FDG-PET has been established through the temporal correlation of regional PET signals (Wehrl et al., 2013; Amend et al., 2019), studies employing transporter or receptor tracers have focused predominantly on interregional binding coherence across subjects using static scans (Lanzenberger et al., 2012; Vanicek et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lanzenberger et al., 2012; Vanicek et al., 2017

claim: The concept and feasibility of molecular connectivity (MC) through the temporal correlation of the dynamic binding potentials of transporter or receptor tracers has yet to be explored.
source: The concept and feasibility of molecular connectivity (MC) (Hahn et al., 2019; Sala et al., 2023) through the temporal correlation of the dynamic binding potentials of transporter or receptor tracers has yet to be explored.

source: In our study, we investigated the feasibility of deriving MC from dynamic [11C]DASB-PET scans acquired simultaneously with fMRI in rats.

source: The baseline cohort assessed the feasibility of the novel methodology, contrasting it with traditional fMRI-derived rs-FC with a specific focus on temporal stability.

source: At the subject level, three molecular and four functional connectomes fell below the threshold of 1 for the small-world coefficient.

claim: Significant consistency was observed between early and late scan-derived connectomes.
source: Significant consistency was observed between early and late scan-derived connectomes (Figure 1D for FC, G for MC), with FC having a slight edge (Figure 1E, r=0.96) over MC (Figure 1H, r=0.8).
evidence: Temporal stability analysis with reference to Figures 1D, 1E, 1G, and 1H

claim: FC has a slight edge (r=0.96) over MC (r=0.8) in consistency between early and late scan-derived connectomes.
source: Significant consistency was observed between early and late scan-derived connectomes (Figure 1D for FC, G for MC), with FC having a slight edge (Figure 1E, r=0.96) over MC (Figure 1H, r=0.8).
evidence: Comparative analysis result with reference to Figures 1E and 1H

claim: Both FC and MC maintained steady correlation intensities with a negligible decline over the scan duration.
source: While both FC and MC maintained steady correlation intensities, there was a negligible decline over the scan duration (Figure 1F and I).

claim: Ten group ICs were extracted from the fMRI data, revealing known canonical resting-state networks.
source: We extracted ten group ICs from the fMRI data (Figure 2A), revealing known canonical resting-state networks, such as the posterior default-mode-like network (IC1-5, red), sensorimotor networks (IC1-5, green and purple), the anterior default-mode-like network (IC6-10, yellow) and the visual network (IC6-10, red).
evidence: ICA analysis result with reference to Figure 2A

claim: Two initial independent components were extracted from MC: IC1 comprising subcortical and cortical anterior brain regions, and IC2 comprising deeper posterior areas.
source: Given the unpredictability of the number of ICs suitable for MC IC extraction, we started with two components (Figure 2B). IC1 (orange) comprised both subcortical and cortical anterior brain regions, including the nucleus accumbens, amygdala, cingulate cortex, caudate putamen, orbitofrontal cortex and medial prefrontal cortex, whereas IC2 (blue) primarily received contributions from deeper posterior areas, such as the midbrain, thalamus, hypothalamus, periaqueductal gray cortex and medulla.
evidence: ICA analysis result with reference to Figure 2B

claim: When 10 independent components were extracted from MC, the initial anterior component split into four different ICs, and the initial posterior IC split into three different ICs.
source: Interestingly, when we extracted 10 independent components to mimic the number of components used for the FC data, the initial anterior component split into four different ICs, and the initial posterior IC split into three different ICs.
evidence: ICA analysis result with reference to Figure 2B

claim: MDMA induced immediate strong decreases in all SERT subcortical network regions, while salience areas exhibited a delay of approximately 10 min.
source: Interestingly, MDMA induced immediate strong decreases in all SERT subcortical network regions, and salience areas exhibited a delay of approximately 10 min (Figure 3A).
evidence: Temporal analysis of MDMA effects with reference to Figure 3A

claim: Voxel-level analysis revealed clear spatial overlaps between early MDMA-responsive regions and those from the posterior IC, with delayed regions mirroring the anterior IC.
source: Voxel-level analysis revealed clear spatial overlaps between early MDMA-responsive regions and those from the posterior IC, with delayed regions mirroring the anterior IC reminiscent of the SERT salience network (Figure 3B).
evidence: Spatial analysis result with reference to Figure 3B

claim: There are highly significant correlations between the z scores of the posterior and anterior ICs and the t scores of late and early MDMA effects on [11C]DASB alterations (p<0.001).
source: To quantify the striking spatial similarity between the baseline independent components and the spatiotemporal characteristics of [11C]DASB changes after MDMA exposure, we found highly significant correlations between the z scores of the posterior and anterior ICs and the t scores of late and early MDMA effects on [11C]DASB alterations (p<0.001, Figure 3C).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis with reference to Figure 3C

claim: The decreases in MC and [11C]DASB BPND following MDMA application showed only a low correlation (r=0.29).
source: We found that the decreases in MC and [11C]DASB BPND following MDMA application (Figure 4A) showed only a low correlation (r=0.29, Figure 4B).
evidence: Correlation analysis result with reference to Figures 4A and 4B

claim: Decreases in SERT availability exhibited a strong anterior-posterior gradient, which was most pronounced in areas with high SERT availability.
source: While decreases in SERT availability exhibited a strong anterior-posterior gradient, which was most pronounced in areas with high SERT availability, such as the MB, VTA, Pons, or PAG, the MC encompassed regions across the brain to similar extents.
evidence: Spatial pattern analysis of MDMA effects

claim: MC encompassed regions across the brain to similar extents following MDMA.
source: While decreases in SERT availability exhibited a strong anterior-posterior gradient, which was most pronounced in areas with high SERT availability, such as the MB, VTA, Pons, or PAG, the MC encompassed regions across the brain to similar extents.

claim: A decrease in salience network FC (16% at the end of the scan, p=0.02) was observed following MDMA, but did not survive FDR correction.
source: We observed a decrease in SN FC (16% at the end of the scan, p=0.02, did not survive FDR correction) and almost constant FC of the subcortical network (<5% decrease, p=0.79) following MDMA, as shown in Figure 5A at the edge and node levels and Figure 5C at the network level.

claim: Almost constant FC of the subcortical network (<5% decrease, p=0.79) was observed following MDMA.
source: We observed a decrease in SN FC (16% at the end of the scan, p=0.02, did not survive FDR correction) and almost constant FC of the subcortical network (<5% decrease, p=0.79) following MDMA, as shown in Figure 5A at the edge and node levels and Figure 5C at the network level.
evidence: Statistical analysis of FC changes with reference to Figures 5A and 5C

claim: Profound reductions in the subcortical network MC (p=0.009) were observed following MDMA.
source: For MC, we observed profound reductions in the subcortical network (Figure 5C and D, p=0.009), emphasizing the acute and spatially specific effect of MDMA on MC.
evidence: Statistical analysis of MC changes with reference to Figures 5C and 5D

claim: The PET data revealed two distinct anatomical components in the serotonergic system: one including key subcortical areas and another comprising regions of the limbic system.
source: In contrast, the PET data revealed two distinct anatomical components in the serotonergic system. One component included key subcortical areas, such as the brainstem, parts of the midbrain, and the thalamus, regions rich in SERT availability and central to serotonergic regulation. The other component comprised regions of the limbic system, such as the striatum, amygdala, insula, cingulate cortex, and prefrontal cortex, critical targets of serotonergic projections from the raphe nuclei.
evidence: Analysis result from the study

claim: These components suggest a broader spatial reach of the serotonergic system than the typically described RSNs, reflecting its unique neurochemical architecture.
source: These components suggest a broader spatial reach of the serotonergic system than the typically described RSNs, reflecting its unique neurochemical architecture.

claim: PET ICs appeared less bilateral than fMRI ICs, likely due to the lower temporal resolution of PET than fMRI.
source: In our analysis, PET ICs appeared less bilateral than fMRI ICs. This is likely due to the lower temporal resolution of PET (80 frames) than of fMRI (2400 frames), resulting in a reduced signal‒to‒noise ratio (SNR) and potentially affecting the stability and symmetry of the independent components.
